title: A Beginner’s Guide to Trigger-Based Workflows
content:
A hypothetical repair shop wants each confirmed service request to create one job card. The demonstration works, but a repeated notification creates a second visit. The missing concept is a definition of one event and one permitted consequence. Trigger-based workflows become manageable when their event, eligibility rule, action, and completion record are explicit.

Separate an event from permission to act

A trigger reports that something happened: a form arrived, a document changed, or a scheduled interval elapsed. An action attempts a consequence. Between them belongs a condition deciding whether this event is eligible. Submitted does not necessarily mean approved, paid, or ready for fulfillment. Those are distinct business states that may require different events and owners.

Write a short contract before opening the automation builder. Identify the source, required fields, destination, and exception owner. For the shop, accept only confirmed requests with an assigned branch. Missing location sends the request to review rather than guessing. This is an editorial design recommendation, not a feature available identically in every platform. Verify the actual product's trigger and filter behavior.

GitHub's trigger documentation illustrates an event-driven system with event selection, filters, and manual inputs. Those controls describe GitHub Actions specifically; use your provider's documentation for its delivery contract.

Give the event and action separate identities

Retain the provider's event identifier where available. Also identify the business object, such as request R-104. One object can produce several legitimate events, so suppressing everything with its identifier might discard later updates. A deduplication key could combine the event identifier with the intended action. Store the key and state where concurrent workers cannot both claim the same operation.

A spreadsheet lookup followed by an append is not automatically atomic. Two workers could both find no result before either writes. For a small internal process, a single worker and manual reconciliation may be sufficient. For inventory or payments, require storage and destination operations that enforce the necessary uniqueness. Ask what happens if execution stops between the destination write and the completion record.

Treat uncertain outcomes as their own state

A timeout means an answer did not arrive. It does not prove the destination did nothing. Blind retrying can repeat a successful write. Prefer a destination with an idempotency mechanism, or a way to find the original operation by a stable reference. When neither exists, send ambiguous outcomes to a human with enough information to investigate before repeating the action.

Separate temporary failures from invalid requests. A temporary outage might justify bounded retries with increasing delays. A rejected address generally needs correction. Set a maximum attempt count, exception queue, and owner. Avoid a loop in which correcting the source repeatedly retriggers the workflow. Keep the original event available for investigation without copying unnecessary personal data into every log entry.

Walk through a hypothetical duplicate

Event E-77 refers to confirmed request R-104. The worker claims E-77:create-job, creates job J-12, and records its identifier. A second delivery finds the completed key and records a duplicate without creating J-13. A different event reporting an approved reschedule updates J-12 instead of creating another visit. The identifiers here are illustrative, not evidence from a real system.

Now interrupt execution after creation but before the completion record. The design needs a recovery answer. A destination reference containing R-104 might let an operator locate the job. If the destination supports neither lookup nor idempotency, document that limitation and reduce the automation's authority. A pending draft is safer to investigate than an irreversible external action whose outcome cannot be determined.

Limit the worker's authority

Use a connection restricted to the required destination or workspace when supported. A job-card creator does not need account administration. Keep credentials outside event payloads and ordinary logs. Record state, identifiers, and useful error categories instead of entire forms containing addresses or private notes. Check exception notifications too: an alert can expose the same information as the original log.

GitHub's secure-use reference discusses minimum token permissions and secret handling for workflows. Apply its platform-specific advice when using Actions; elsewhere inspect the equivalent permission and credential controls rather than assuming identical behavior.

First-workflow checklist

  • Name the business state permitting each write.
  • Exercise an eligible event, incomplete event, and duplicate.
  • Define the recovery procedure for an uncertain timeout.
  • Retain the destination operation identifier.
  • Assign a maximum retry count and exception owner.
  • Check whether source edits create a trigger loop.
  • Inspect credential scope and notification contents.
  • Provide a pause control that preserves history.

Begin with reviewable internal records before authorizing expensive or irreversible effects. Maintain a reconciliation view of received events, completed actions, and unresolved outcomes. Investigate discrepancies without assuming every missing event is a failure: the provider may filter events before delivery. Your own execution history cannot prove what the source never sent. Describe that boundary and the manual fallback in the operating notes.

When the shop changes its form, recheck the field mapping and eligibility conditions before resuming normal processing. A renamed status can quietly stop valid work or admit invalid work. Keep a small synthetic example for each important state so the owner can inspect a revised mapping without sending real customer requests. Review the pause and recovery controls alongside the happy path. Include the date and reason for the mapping change in the workflow record, and tell the exception owner which queued events require another look before they are released.
